paper.abstract:
Abstract We study the problem of fair ranking in recommender systems. We provide a
formal probabilistic framework in which ranking policies are distributions
over permutations, and the utility of a user is the exposure given to the
items they interact with, relative to that of an ideal ranking. We consider utility parity across user groups, as well as its category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which requires parity within each category of items. Following a recent view of fairness
as distributional stability, we show that both criteria are equivalent to
the stability of the utility under changes in the composition of user
groups. Optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies leads to a second-order
cone program, for which we provide generalization bounds. A numerical study
validates our theoretical findings.

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Recommender Systems (RS), often trained as learning-to-rank models, play an increasing role in access to opportunities. On job platforms, the offers displayed to a candidate are ordered according to their predicted relevance to the candidate’s profile. When trained on historical interaction data, these models can reproduce disparities related to sensitive attributes such as gender. For example, women may see fewer high-paying or high-responsibility positions than men ( Imana et al., 2021 ) . Since candidates primarily interact with the highest-ranked offers, what each user sees at the top of their ranking determines the quality of service they receive, and can ultimately affect their career path. A natural answer is to require comparable utility across user groups, where the utility of a ranking measures how much exposure it gives to the offers the user is interested in. We refer to this criterion as utility parity. Existing works on user-side fairness in recommendation compare a single utility, aggregated over all offers ( Li et al., 2021 ; Wang and Joachims, 2021 ; Yao and Huang, 2017 ) . Such aggregate parity can be misleading: a ranking model may satisfy it while favouring one group on some categories of offers, such as administrative positions, and the other group on others, such as managerial positions, so that the gaps cancel out in aggregate. A similar phenomenon is known in classification, where parity on a population can hide disparities within its subgroups ( Kearns et al., 2018 ) . Recent work has pointed out this limitation and proposed item category-aware criteria ( Kheya et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Parity, whether aggregate or per category, also has a dynamic reading. On a job platform, the share of women among job seekers may change over time, for instance when the platform opens to new sectors or regions, and as long as a gap remains, the average quality of the recommendations rises or falls with this balance. We build on this reading, drawing inspiration from Taturyan et al. (2026) , who view fairness in classification as the stability of a prediction rate under perturbations of group proportions, and learn fair classifiers as mixtures of reweighted predictors. Extending this view to ranking is far from straightforward, due to the global nature of this learning task. For each observation, a classifier predicts a label, which can be modified without changing the other predicted labels. In contrast, a ranking policy organizes the entire catalogue: each item is assigned a specific position in the list, so that its exposure depends on the position of all other items. And changing the rank of one item can affect the rank of (possibly many) other items. We therefore represent ranking policies through the exposure they allocate. The utility of a user then depends linearly on this exposure, so that average utility plays the role of the prediction rate, and the utility of a mixture of policies is exactly the mixture of their utilities. The stability view thus carries over to ranking, and the resulting problem is solved exactly over mixtures of policies, whereas in classification the risk of a mixture is handled through a surrogate. The framework has several benefits. First, since the utility of a ranking is additive over the offers it contains, it decomposes according to their category, and category-aware constraints arise naturally in this formulation, leading to what we call conditional utility parity. Second, utility parity is equivalent to the stability of utility under changes in the proportion of each user group, so that the guarantees hold uniformly over a range of group compositions. Third, the constraints can include a target of utility level per category, which prevents parity from being reached by lowering the utility that both groups derive from a category. Contributions First, we provide a formal probabilistic framework for recommendation setup (Section 2 ). Second, we formalize utility parity and conditional utility parity as stability properties, which yields a constraint controlling both the group gap and the utility level (Section 3 ). Third, considering mixtures of policies, we write the empirical problem as a second-order cone program (Section 4 ) and discuss its feasibility. Fourth, we provide finite-sample guarantees on fairness, deployment stability and utility, with explicit exposure rates for Plackett–Luce policies (Section 5 ). Finally, we conduct numerical experiments that confirm our theory in practice (Section 6 ). Related Works There is a large amount of literature on fair ranking, most of which focus on item-side fairness through allocated exposure. A seminal work of Singh and Joachims (2018) formulates fairness of exposure as a linear program over doubly stochastic matrices, from which stochastic rankings are sampled through a Birkhoff–von Neumann decomposition. Wang and Joachims (2021) build on this approach to enforce user fairness, item fairness and diversity together: they optimize both notions of fairness as a convex program, and derive the ranking policy through a new decomposition algorithm. Exposure-based fairness has also been integrated in the training of ranking policies, by backpropagating through constrained optimization problems ( Kotary et al., 2022 ; Dinh et al., 2024 ) , or through efficient gradient estimators for Plackett–Luce policies ( Oosterhuis, 2021 ) . Closest to our work are the category-aware criteria of Kheya et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2024) . Kheya et al. (2025) compare the share of each category in the top- K K lists of men and women and use the resulting gap as a regularizer during training. Wang et al. (2024) require a recall-based metric of relevant items to be similar across all pairs of user and item groups, and reweight the training losses with a variant of group distributionally robust optimization. Our criteria differ from both. Unlike the former, our utility only rewards exposure to relevant offers. Unlike the latter, we compare user groups within each category, without asking categories to be treated equally. Overall, despite the rich literature, most fair ranking methods are algorithmic and empirical, and do not rely on a probabilistic framework that would allow for statistical guarantees. The existing guarantees are mostly of a different nature. For example, fair rank aggregation algorithms come with approximation guarantees which bound how far their solution can be from the optimum ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ; Chakraborty et al., 2026 ; Chakraborty et al., 2025 ) . Statistical guarantees have been provided in other setups, for instance in learning to rank, where a stochastic ranker built on a pretrained model is calibrated post hoc to guarantee a target level of utility, while item-exposure fairness is improved but not guaranteed ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , or in recommendation, where an online bandit algorithm decides with high probability whether some user would prefer another user’s recommendations, without degrading the audited system’s performance by more than a fixed fraction ( Do et al., 2022 ) . In contrast, we provide finite-sample guarantees on both the user-side category-aware fairness and the utility of a learned ranking policy, with fairness gaps and utility levels controlled uniformly over a range of group compositions. As a result, we observe a clear trade-off curve between utility and fairness, which methods without guarantees cannot ensure. sections.heading: 6.1 Synthetic Data
sections.text: Setup We simulate a simplified job platform with 8000 8000 users, and a catalogue of 300 300 offers divided into three categories: managerial ( A A ), administrative ( B B ) and other ( C C ). The true interests of users do not depend on their group, so an oracle policy has no gap in any category. The policies are however learned from biased historical interactions: with probability β \beta , an interest of a woman in a managerial offer, or of a man in an administrative offer, was not recorded. The constraints are estimated, and the policies evaluated, on held-out users labelled with their true interests. To illustrate the deployment guarantee, we also evaluate them on new users drawn with a share of women between 0.1 0.1 and 0.9 0.9 . The results, deferred to Appendix D.2 , are in line with Theorem 1 . The data generation is detailed in Appendix D.2 . Policies and constraints The dictionary contains the uniform policy, an unweighted LambdaMART ranker P 0 P_{0} , and five LambdaMART rankers trained with the weights w ξ w_{\xi} , ξ ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 } \xi\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\} . Rankers are trained with LightGBM on PureSVD embeddings of the history, and the sensitive attribute is never used as a feature. Policies rank deterministically, and the utility is the NDCG@20 (Remark 1 ). We solve ( ^ P ) with Ξ \Xi uniform on [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] [0.1,0.9] . The budgets δ a \delta_{a} are set so that the tolerated gap in each category is λ \lambda times the estimation noise of the gap of P 0 P_{0} , with λ = 1 \lambda=1 unless stated otherwise. sections.heading: 6.2 MovieLens-1M
sections.text: Set-up and baselines We use MovieLens-1M with gender as the sensitive attribute ( G = 1 G=1 for women). Item categories are the six movie genres (Sci-Fi, Adventure, Crime, Romance, Children’s, Horror), and we keep the movies that belong to exactly one of them. The interactions of each user are sorted by time: the first 80% form the history 𝒙 {\bm{x}} and the remaining 20% are the relevant items. The candidates of a user are all movies outside their history. Users are split at random into training (50%), estimation (25%), on which the mixture weights are fitted, and test (25%) users, and results are averaged over 10 random splits. Statistics are given in Appendix D.3 . We compare with ITFR ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and CatFAIR ( Kheya et al., 2025 ) , which, like CUP, consider disparities between (user group, item category) pairs: ITFR through a recall-based measure of relevant items, CatFAIR through the share of each category in the recommendation lists, regardless of relevance. Both modify the training of a matrix factorization model with the BPR loss ( Rendle et al., 2009 ) , see the same interactions as the rankers, and use G G during training only. Each is compared with its own backbone trained without the fairness component (MF-BPR for ITFR, α = 0 \alpha=0 for CatFAIR), as P 0 P_{0} is for our approach. The dictionary of Section 6.1 is enriched with several rankers to improve feasibility. In the end, we consider L = 19 L=19 , detailed in Table 2 (Appendix D.3 )). Targets are t a = κ ​ Φ a ​ ( P 0 , μ Ξ ) t_{a}=\kappa\,\Phi_{a}(P_{0};\mu_{\Xi}) , and κ \kappa varies from 1 1 to 0.8 0.8 to trace the trade-off between utility and gaps, with λ = 2 \lambda=2 , the smallest budget of our grid for which the targets with κ ≤ 0.9 \kappa\leq 0.9 can be met on every split. CUP without target uses λ ∈ { 1.5 , 2 , 3 } \lambda\in\{1.5,2,3\} . On the test users, we report the utility, the largest category gap max a ⁡ | γ a | \max_{a}|\gamma_{a}| , and the worst-case utility loss 1 − min a ⁡ min ξ ​ Φ a ​ ( P , ξ ) / min ξ ⁡ Φ a ​ ( Backbone , ξ ) 1-\min_{a}\min_{\xi}\Phi_{a}(P;\xi)/\min_{\xi}\Phi_{a}(\text{Backbone};\xi) , which measures how much the less-served population loses in the most affected category. Utility and fairness. We see from Figure 2 that CUP, ITFR and CatFAIR all reduce the gaps between women and men across genres with respect to their backbones, which start from different levels of utility, P 0 P_{0} being the most accurate. The three approaches differ in how the trade-off is controlled. First, ITFR gives a single operating point, as none of its hyperparameters sets the trade-off ( Wang et al., 2024 , App. A.4) . CatFAIR reaches its smallest gap with the smallest weight α \alpha , and larger values only lower utility (a). CUP instead traces a front: lowering κ \kappa reduces the largest gap at the cost of utility, and any point of this front is obtained in milliseconds from the same dictionary. Second, the targets prevent levelling down (b). Without targets, CUP reaches the same utility and largest gap, but the less-served group loses much more utility in the most affected genre. So does CatFAIR, which ignores relevance, with the weight used by its authors. Now turning to the question of which movie genres are affected, we see from Figure 2 (c) that the three methods reduce the gaps in different ways. CUP narrows the gap of P 0 P_{0} in every genre and changes the utility of each genre by less than 10 % 10\% . ITFR moves utility across genres, from − 21 % -21\% for Sci-Fi to + 51 % +51\% for Horror, where the gap widens. CatFAIR closes the gaps in Romance and Children’s, but by lowering the utility of women in these genres, which is halved in Romance. Choosing the trade-off in practice. For a practitioner, the level of fairness is a choice that must be made after seeing its cost in utility, and possibly revised: an explicit front is therefore as important as the quality of a single operating point. Our guarantees are what make such a front reliable: the budgets and targets set the gaps and utility levels directly, and Theorem 1 ensures that these settings carry over to new users, whereas ITFR and CatFAIR control fairness only through training hyperparameters, with no guarantee on the resulting gaps. With CUP, the dictionary is trained once (about 2 2 min per split), and each point of the front, set by interpretable targets, is a second-order cone program solved in less than 10 10 ms. With ITFR and CatFAIR, each point requires a full training (about 38 38 and 2 min on the same CPU), and finding the trade-off means cross-validating hyperparameters whose effects on fairness are not monotone.

sections.heading: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.text: We studied user-side category-aware fair ranking through the lens of distributional stability. Representing ranking policies through exposure, we showed that utility parity and its category-aware refinement can be viewed as the stability of utility under changes in the composition of the population, and that targets fix the level of service that each category keeps, whatever this composition. Considering mixtures of policies leads to a second-order cone program, for which we provided finite-sample guarantees on stability, fairness, deployment and utility. Since it only combines existing ranking policies, the approach is model-agnostic: it can be applied on top of the most accurate ranker available, and the trade-off between utility and fairness can be set, and revised, after training at negligible cost. Our experiments showed that aggregate parity can hide opposite disparities across categories, which conditional utility parity removes, illustrated the deployment guarantee on new populations, and showed that the targets give an explicit control of the trade-off while limiting levelling down. Our guarantees cover changes in the share of each group; changes in the behaviour of each group are left for future work.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.40182v1 [stat.ML] 29 Oct 2026 Hidden Disparities in Ranking: Category-Aware Fairness via Distributional Stability Gayane Taturyan Charlotte Laclau Stephan Clémençon LTCI, Télécom Paris Institut Polytechnique de Paris, France Abstract We study the problem of fair ranking in recommender systems. We provide a formal probabilistic framework in which ranking policies are distributions over permutations, and the utility of a user is the exposure given to the items they interact with, relative to that of an ideal ranking. We consider utility parity across user groups, as well as its category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which requires parity within each category of items. Following a recent view of fairness as distributional stability, we show that both criteria are equivalent to the stability of the utility under changes in the composition of user groups. Optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies leads to a second-order cone program, for which we provide generalization bounds. A numerical study validates our theoretical findings. 1 INTRODUCTION Recommender Systems (RS), often trained as learning-to-rank models, play an increasing role in access to opportunities. On job platforms, the offers displayed to a candidate are ordered according to their predicted relevance to the candidate’s profile. When trained on historical interaction data, these models can reproduce disparities related to sensitive attributes such as gender. For example, women may see fewer high-paying or high-responsibility positions than men ( Imana et al., 2021 ) . Since candidates primarily interact with the highest-ranked offers, what each user sees at the top of their ranking determines the quality of service they receive, and can ultimately affect their career path. A natural answer is to require comparable utility across user groups, where the utility of a ranking measures how much exposure it gives to the offers the user is interested in. We refer to this criterion as utility parity. Existing works on user-side fairness in recommendation compare a single utility, aggregated over all offers ( Li et al., 2021 ; Wang and Joachims, 2021 ; Yao and Huang, 2017 ) . Such aggregate parity can be misleading: a ranking model may satisfy it while favouring one group on some categories of offers, such as administrative positions, and the other group on others, such as managerial positions, so that the gaps cancel out in aggregate. A similar phenomenon is known in classification, where parity on a population can hide disparities within its subgroups ( Kearns et al., 2018 ) . Recent work has pointed out this limitation and proposed item category-aware criteria ( Kheya et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Parity, whether aggregate or per category, also has a dynamic reading. On a job platform, the share of women among job seekers may change over time, for instance when the platform opens to new sectors or regions, and as long as a gap remains, the average quality of the recommendations rises or falls with this balance. We build on this reading, drawing inspiration from Taturyan et al. (2026) , who view fairness in classification as the stability of a prediction rate under perturbations of group proportions, and learn fair classifiers as mixtures of reweighted predictors. Extending this view to ranking is far from straightforward, due to the global nature of this learning task. For each observation, a classifier predicts a label, which can be modified without changing the other predicted labels. In contrast, a ranking policy organizes the entire catalogue: each item is assigned a specific position in the list, so that its exposure depends on the position of all other items. And changing the rank of one item can affect the rank of (possibly many) other items. We therefore represent ranking policies through the exposure they allocate. The utility of a user then depends linearly on this exposure, so that average utility plays the role of the prediction rate, and the utility of a mixture of policies is exactly the mixture of their utilities. The stability view thus carries over to ranking, and the resulting problem is solved exactly over mixtures of policies, whereas in classification the risk of a mixture is handled through a surrogate. The framework has several benefits. First, since the utility of a ranking is additive over the offers it contains, it decomposes according to their category, and category-aware constraints arise naturally in this formulation, leading to what we call conditional utility parity. Second, utility parity is equivalent to the stability of utility under changes in the proportion of each user group, so that the guarantees hold uniformly over a range of group compositions. Third, the constraints can include a target of utility level per category, which prevents parity from being reached by lowering the utility that both groups derive from a category. Contributions First, we provide a formal probabilistic framework for recommendation setup (Section 2 ). Second, we formalize utility parity and conditional utility parity as stability properties, which yields a constraint controlling both the group gap and the utility level (Section 3 ). Third, considering mixtures of policies, we write the empirical problem as a second-order cone program (Section 4 ) and discuss its feasibility. Fourth, we provide finite-sample guarantees on fairness, deployment stability and utility, with explicit exposure rates for Plackett–Luce policies (Section 5 ). Finally, we conduct numerical experiments that confirm our theory in practice (Section 6 ). Related Works There is a large amount of literature on fair ranking, most of which focus on item-side fairness through allocated exposure. A seminal work of Singh and Joachims (2018) formulates fairness of exposure as a linear program over doubly stochastic matrices, from which stochastic rankings are sampled through a Birkhoff–von Neumann decomposition. Wang and Joachims (2021) build on this approach to enforce user fairness, item fairness and diversity together: they optimize both notions of fairness as a convex program, and derive the ranking policy through a new decomposition algorithm. Exposure-based fairness has also been integrated in the training of ranking policies, by backpropagating through constrained optimization problems ( Kotary et al., 2022 ; Dinh et al., 2024 ) , or through efficient gradient estimators for Plackett–Luce policies ( Oosterhuis, 2021 ) . Closest to our work are the category-aware criteria of Kheya et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2024) . Kheya et al. (2025) compare the share of each category in the top- K K lists of men and women and use the resulting gap as a regularizer during training. Wang et al. (2024) require a recall-based metric of relevant items to be similar across all pairs of user and item groups, and reweight the training losses with a variant of group distributionally robust optimization. Our criteria differ from both. Unlike the former, our utility only rewards exposure to relevant offers. Unlike the latter, we compare user groups within each category, without asking categories to be treated equally. Overall, despite the rich literature, most fair ranking methods are algorithmic and empirical, and do not rely on a probabilistic framework that would allow for statistical guarantees. The existing guarantees are mostly of a different nature. For example, fair rank aggregation algorithms come with approximation guarantees which bound how far their solution can be from the optimum ( Chakraborty et al., 2022 ; Chakraborty et al., 2026 ; Chakraborty et al., 2025 ) . Statistical guarantees have been provided in other setups, for instance in learning to rank, where a stochastic ranker built on a pretrained model is calibrated post hoc to guarantee a target level of utility, while item-exposure fairness is improved but not guaranteed ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , or in recommendation, where an online bandit algorithm decides with high probability whether some user would prefer another user’s recommendations, without degrading the audited system’s performance by more than a fixed fraction ( Do et al., 2022 ) . In contrast, we provide finite-sample guarantees on both the user-side category-aware fairness and the utility of a learned ranking policy, with fairness gaps and utility levels controlled uniformly over a range of group compositions. As a result, we observe a clear trade-off curve between utility and fairness, which methods without guarantees cannot ensure.
